descriptive_title: Grade 1 Mathematics: Algebra — Identifying Change vs Constant Quantities, Testing Equivalence, and Using Equivalent Relationships for Numbers to 50 (C2.1–C2.3)
subject: Mathematics

curriculum_expectations.C2.1: identify quantities that can change and quantities that always remain the same in real-life contexts
curriculum_expectations.C2.2: determine whether given pairs of addition and subtraction expressions are equivalent or not
curriculum_expectations.C2.3: identify and use equivalent relationships for whole numbers up to 50, in various contexts

unit_overview: A 5-day Grade 1 unit on Algebra framed around 'Balance Scale Stories' — Bella the Balance Beam Scientist and Bobby her Balance Beam Buddy. Day 1 introduces the IDEA of change vs constant in real-life: classroom population changes daily, the number of legs on a chair stays at 4 (C2.1). Day 2 introduces the balance scale as a physical model: equal expressions balance, unequal ones tip (C2.2). Day 3 extends to including unknown values: 4 + ? = 7 means we need 3 to balance. Day 4 hunts for equivalent expressions to numbers up to 50 (10 = 5+5, 4+6, 8+2, 0+10) (C2.3). Day 5 closes with child-created balance stories linking algebra to real life. The unit progresses concrete (real or pretend balance scale) → representational (drawn balance scales with quantities on each side) → abstract (equivalence equations).
unit_learning_goal: Children will identify quantities that change and quantities that stay the same; determine whether addition and subtraction expressions are equivalent; and find equivalent relationships for whole numbers up to 50.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Some quantities CHANGE (people in class, weather); others STAY THE SAME (10 fingers, 4 corners).
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can name things that change and things that stay the same in my life.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Bella sorts photo cards into 'CHANGE' and 'STAY THE SAME' columns; partner discussion of classroom examples.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Two expressions can be equal (the SAME amount) or not equal. A balance scale shows it: equal = level; not equal = tipped.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can decide if two addition or subtraction expressions are equal.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Balance scale demos: 5+3 vs 4+4 (equal), 5+3 vs 9 (equal), 5+3 vs 6+3 (not equal); equality vs inequality vocabulary.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Knowing one side of the balance lets me find the missing number. 4 + ? = 7 means 3.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can find the missing number that makes two expressions equal.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Missing-addend puzzles on the balance: 4 + ? = 7; ? + 5 = 9; ? - 2 = 4; whole-class balance balancing.

lesson_arc.big_idea: There are many ways to make the same amount. 10 = 5+5 = 4+6 = 8+2 = 0+10 = 11-1. Equivalent expressions name the same number.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can find many equivalent expressions for the same whole number up to 50.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Equivalent-expression hunt for target numbers (10, 25, 50); record on a chart; partner-share results.

lesson_arc.big_idea: We can use balance ideas to tell stories about real life. Bella and Bobby balance jars of buttons, kids on a teeter-totter, and recipe ingredients.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can tell a balance story about something in real life and write the equation.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Children invent a balance story (e.g., '4 friends on the seesaw, 4 friends on the other side — balanced!') and draw + write the equation.

recurring_characters.name: Bella the Balance Beam Scientist
recurring_characters.role: Lead character. A young scientist in a lab coat with a beaker patch. Anchors all 5 lessons. Loves balance scales and 'is it equal?' questions.
recurring_characters.visual_description: A young Grade-1er in a small lab coat with a balance-scale patch on the chest, eyeglasses, neat bobbed hair, eager smile, holding a small paper balance scale.

recurring_characters.name: Bobby the Balance Beam Buddy
recurring_characters.role: Bella's partner. The 'check-it' character — when Bella claims something is equal, Bobby checks with the scale. Cameo Lessons 2-5.
recurring_characters.visual_description: A young Grade-1er with a striped shirt and a tool-belt holding a small toy balance scale. Curious expression, slight grin, hair tousled.

threaded_vocabulary.child_friendly_definition: Something that can be different. The number of students in class can change every day.
Something that does not change. A square has 4 sides — that always stays the same.
The same amount. 5 + 3 is equal to 8.
When two amounts are the same, the balance scale stays level. When they're different, it tips.
A math sentence with numbers and operations. 5 + 3 is an expression. 8 is also an expression.
The number we don't know yet. In 4 + ? = 7, the missing number is 3.
Equal in value. 5 + 3 and 4 + 4 are equivalent because they both equal 8.

assessment_strategy.diagnostic: Lesson 1 change-or-stay snapshot: each child sorts 6 photo cards into 'change' and 'stay the same'. Tally accuracy.
assessment_strategy.formative: Lesson 2 equivalence tracker; Lesson 3 missing-number tracker; Lesson 4 equivalent-expressions tracker.
assessment_strategy.summative: Lesson 5 Balance Story worksheet — children invent a story and write 2 equivalent expressions. Captures C2.1, C2.2, C2.3 in one creative artifact.

pedagogical_notes: C2.1 is conceptual — distinguishing change from stay-the-same is foundational for the variable concept later.
C2.2 builds on Grade 1's addition/subtraction work. The balance scale is the embodied form of the equal sign.
C2.3 ties algebra to fluency with numbers — for any target up to 50, children should generate multiple equivalent expressions.
The equal sign (=) means SAME AMOUNT — not 'gives you the answer'. This is the critical Grade-1 insight. 5 + 3 = 8 doesn't mean '5 and 3 give you 8'; it means '5 + 3 is the SAME AS 8'.
Balance scales make the equal sign physical. Use them as much as possible.
canadian_context_notes: Real-life examples: number of NHL teams (changes — Vegas added in 2017), number of provinces (stays at 10), number of seasons in a year (stays at 4), number of toonies in your pocket (changes).
Recipes can be balance metaphors: 1 cup flour = 1 cup flour (regardless of how many times you make pancakes).
Classroom routine examples: number of helpers today (changes), number of days in October (stays — 31).
